A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Grendel research work. All 20 pages of each version, including equations, figures, tables, and appendices, are readable and support reliable matching across relocations and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction-quality, training-throughput, memory-scaling, and optimization experiments in Sections 4–5 and Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original CityGaussian comparisons, workload visualization, timing breakdowns, and rendering-speed measurements.

M1.justification: Gaussian-wise and pixel-wise partitioning, sparse all-to-all communication, iterative load balancing, and the Adam scaling rules remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 gains an explicit description of its runtime-estimate input, but its operations are identical.

E1.justification: Section 5.3 adds the Building scene to the large-scene reconstruction evaluation. The original datasets and tasks remain covered; downsampling retained scenes changes preprocessing rather than dataset coverage.

E2.justification: v1 mainly compares Grendel's own GPU, batch-size, and component configurations. v2 adds a substantive external comparison against CityGaussian across three scenes, using its official configuration and a matched 200K-image budget (Section 5.3, Table 2). DOGS and RetinaGS are discussed but not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: The new CityGaussian evaluation introduces four-A100 comparisons, fourfold downsampling of Rubble and Building, a 1600-pixel width for MatrixCity, and official versus matched 200K-image training budgets. Appendix C.4 separately introduces forward-rendering measurements with one image at a time on one versus four GPUs. Existing experiments retain their reported settings.

E4.justification: New Figure 4 visualizes per-tile Gaussian workload imbalance on Train, and Table 10 decomposes CityGaussian's runtime into coarse training, partitioning, cell training, and merging. Existing optimization and load-balancing ablations are retained, with several moved to the appendices.

E5.justification: The gradient analysis still reports averaging over 32 random trials (v1 Figure 5; v2 Figure 6). No new seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-reporting practices accompany the added benchmark results.

E6.justification: The original numerical tables are retained, while v2 adds substantial comparative and rendering results. For example, Table 2 reports downsampled Rubble PSNR/time of 27.39/0.85 hours for Grendel versus 25.40/2.18 hours for CityGS at matched 200K-image budgets. Table 11 adds Rubble rendering rates of 8.8 and 21.7 images/s on one and four GPUs. These are newly reported results under their specified settings.

T1.justification: The independent-gradient and zero-mean assumptions, Adam update derivation, square-root learning-rate rule, and exponential momentum rule are mathematically unchanged. Revised attribution and explanatory wording introduce no new proof or formal result.

C1.justification: The abstract and three central contributions retain the same system, scaling strategy, and headline Rubble result. The introduction now presents earlier large-scene approaches as complementary rather than uniformly constrained by single-GPU limitations; the conclusion's unqualified claim of nearly perfect performance and memory scalability is removed.

C2.justification: Section 5.3 adds interpretations about convergence efficiency and workflow simplicity relative to CityGaussian. The discussion also explains how Grendel could accelerate existing coarse-training pipelines and distinguishes potential convergence or redundant-computation issues in DOGS and RetinaGS. Existing gradient-independence qualifications remain.

D1.justification: The expanded Figure 12 caption specifies which learning-rate or momentum rule is held fixed in each existing ablation. v2 also supplies the CityGaussian script reference and stagewise training times, and adds a reproducibility statement promising Rubble and MatrixCity checkpoints. These are documentation and release-plan additions, not evidence of a changed core implementation.

R1.justification: v2 substantially revises positioning: it adds a distributed-3DGS discussion covering DOGS and RetinaGS, treats divide-and-conquer and level-of-detail methods as complementary, and explicitly attributes the Adam scaling motivation to Malladi et al. The neural-network distributed-training discussion moves to Appendix D. References to the surge phenomenon and SGD–SDE validity work are removed.

P1.justification: The introduction and optimization motivation are rewritten, the main ablation section moves to Appendix C.1, and distributed-neural-network related work moves to Appendix D. The conclusion is removed, a reproducibility statement is added, and the appendix structure is expanded. This substantially reorganizes the narrative despite retaining the core method.

P2.justification: The document is extensively reformatted into the ICLR layout. v2 adds a workload heatmap and three tables, reformats the Gaussian-intersection illustration, and relocates optimization, memory-scaling, load-balancing, and qualitative reconstruction figures into the appendices. Existing exhibits are also resized, reflowed, and recaptioned.

improvement.justification: v1 made strong comparative claims largely through Grendel's own scaling experiments. v2 addresses this important evidence gap with direct CityGaussian comparisons using both official and matched training budgets, supported by detailed timing breakdowns (Tables 2 and 10). Clearer attribution, complementary positioning, and documented ablation controls further strengthen the paper. The new comparisons use downsampled scenes and do not establish superiority at every resolution, but they substantially improve comparative validation.
